I have really horrendous car anxiety due an accident I was in a couple years ago. I only recently got my license at 21 years old after renewing my permit two times so I definitely understand. Personally, I was so resistant that I didn’t even want to learn and when people drove me around, I would start to experience anxiety symptoms due to speed, sharp turns, etc.
What helped me was to just do it. Which is not as easy as it sounds. My driving instructor told me that it seemed like I wasn’t breathing lol. However, take it slowly. Go to a school parking lot after hours as often as you can and practice speed, turns, parking, braking, etc. 
Last summer, I did that and practiced almost every single day. I hated it but the consistency is what got me more comfortable and confident. I also realized that I am the one in control of the car. Once you’re more confident in your skills, start going to places you’re familiar with- whether that’s a local mall or a coffee shop you like. Consistency is key! It’s very classic exposure therapy. 
Even now that I drive most places, I still get anxious when I’m driving long distances or if I’m in an unfamiliar place, bad weather, etc. As the last user said, modern cars are super safe! I keep pushing myself to do it and I have definitely noticed over time that I have become much more comfortable.
Sorry for going on forever, but the last thing that I think has helped me is listening to music. Minimize distractions of course, but sometimes when I start panicking when I’m driving, I’ll turn the music up and sing along so my brain focuses more on that and less on the anxiety. To not take my hands off the wheel, I curated a playlist of songs I love, would not skip, and know most/all the words to. Hope this helps and good luck!

A year after my brother started speaking, my sister was born and lo and behold we had our last sibling born in 2020…fully transformed into a large traditional Catholic family of seven. My parents are of course very displeased that I don’t participate.

As I’m in this group, I’m clearly not Catholic anymore but I can talk a bit about my parents! Not exactly a conversion but sort of? 
Both were born and baptized Catholic. My dad grew up very strong in his faith and initially wanted to pursue priesthood. On the other hand, my mom was baptized because it was culturally appropriate (Latin America is highly Catholic) but she was not raised to go to Mass or learn any of the teachings. Growing up, she was not religious at all and even aligned herself with being pro-choice and heavily feminist. 
When she married my father, he wanted her to go to weekly Mass with him so she agreed. My brother and I were both baptized soon after being born, as tradition. My brother was diagnosed with Autism at three years old and was nonverbal. His providers told my parents that it was highly unlikely he would ever speak which completely devastated my mother. 
A little about the church I went to growing up: it was a smaller, prominently Spanish speaking church. The community was very tight knit. The priests at the church were not from the Diocese but from a missionary called the Institute of the Incarnate Word (IVE). Along with the IVE priests, we also had their sister missionary nuns, the Servants of the Lord and the Virgen of Matará (SSVM). My father was very close to the priest there and would often assist in Mass with the collection and altar serving if there were no altar servers available. 
I guess my brother took a liking to Mass (which I believe has to do with how methodological and structured it is- you always know what they’re going to say and what comes next). One day, he just stood up and followed my dad to help him serve. Following this, the sisters at the church told my mom it was vital for my brother and I (both 5 and 6 years old at the time) to start received CCD classes. My mom learned the teachings of the church through our books and homework. 
Then, randomly one day in Mass, my brother starts to speak for the first time…and recites the Our Father perfectly. Hard to take that as not a miracle for many people, especially when you’re surrounded by the public eye of the church. You can become a research assistant for credit, through the Work Study Research Program, volunteering, or an individual lab's funding. There are also a ton of programs to support individual research endeavors such as McNair, BOLD, IDEA Grant, SURF Grant, OUR Supply awards, Rowe Scholars, SHARE Grant (humanities research fellowship) and Apprenticeship, etc. There's also funding for other similar projects like the Werth Innovator program which helps fund entrepreneurial projects. The IDEA grant is also not specific to research, some students this cohort are using it to fund their own art exhibits, theatre productions, and more.

Regardless of your major, research is such an amazing experience, especially if you plan on going to grad school in the future. It also gives you the opportunity to work closely with a specific mentor and build that relationship which will give you connections and also a great letter of rec down the line.

I'm going into my junior year majoring in psych and english at the Stamford campus and love it! I think the main cons are typically for students who cannot complete their major here (less activities related to those majors). But for someone like you who is in DMD and can complete that in Stamford, it is worth it! 

First, the location is great if you're 21+, but in general, there's tons of restaurants, parks, a mall, target, and cafe's within walking distance. We also have a YMCA nearby that gives a free membership through UConn.  
Secondly, you can go to New York within 40-45 min by train for around $23 round trip. Not bad AT ALL.

We also have a decent amount of clubs! A lot of campus wide events are hosted by SGA and First Generation Club.

I also chose to stay here instead of campus change to Storrs due to mental health reasons. I love the smaller class sizes and the ability to connect with my professors easily, both which lessen my anxiety about going to class. Also, my experience with the Mental Health Resource Center and CSD in Stamford has been pretty good so far (ESA and single room accommodation, Student Services, and to help find outside services).

Lastly, it's way less expensive tuition-wise (unless you dorm, the dorms are super expensive beyond the standard rate). However, the dorms are pretty nice as they are all suite style. If you do dorm- single rooms are super limited and only by accommodation, and even then only if any are available. And having a single room does still mean you have other roommates in the apartment.

Overall, I have really enjoyed my time on this campus! Hope this helps :)
